Someone good at trivia is more likely to be right. But being likely is not the same as being checked, and even good memories slip.

A group chat is easy to check, but people who join it share a lot, and those who disagree may stay silent. It tells you something about the chat, not the school.

Yes. Comparing the same students with and without breakfast takes out many differences between people, and gets closer to the question of cause.
Eating breakfast is harmless for most people, so advising it is low-risk. But the advice is not evidence that breakfast raises scores, and it should not be presented as if it were.
connections.notes: Harmless advice, not a test of the claim.

connections.feedback: The study shows that two things go together, not why. Jumping to cause skips other explanations.

Scheduling calls on Tuesdays costs little and doubles as a test. But it can also lock in a habit before the pattern is shown, and you may miss better days.
connections.notes: Cheap and testable; may lock in a habit too early.

connections.feedback: With a handful of cases, chance can easily cluster. Calling the day lucky explains something that may not need explaining.

connections.feedback: Yes. You owe the listener an honest picture of how much you know. Saying what you saw, how long ago, and how it went lets them weigh it and does not claim more than you have.
Saying nothing avoids overclaiming. It also withholds a real piece of positive information, and leaves your colleague without a fair hearing.
One good project long ago is not a basis for a strong recommendation. People will rely on your word, so overclaiming can cost them.
Saying you do not remember is untrue. It dodges the question rather than answering it honestly.

connections.feedback: Yes. A missing theme tells you the summary is incomplete in at least one way, and there may be others. Checking against a sample of the raw comments tells you how far to trust it before leadership acts on it.
Adding what you know is useful and quick. But you cannot tell how many other themes are missing, so the whole summary stays unchecked.
connections.notes: Fixes the one gap you know about; leaves others unseen.

connections.feedback: You already know the summary has a gap. Presenting it as complete would pass that gap on to the people making decisions.
